# About

URL: https://kompositenews.com/about/

About Komposite News
Komposite News is an independent digital publication covering artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital assets, enterprise technology, cybersecurity, fintech and capital markets. We write for executives, founders, investors, developers and policy professionals who need to understand how technology and finance are changing each other.
Our coverage prioritizes reporting and analysis over hype. We are interested in what is being built, what it costs, who is buying it and what the consequences are, and we hold breathless claims from any direction to the same standard of evidence.
Ownership and funding: Komposite News is independently operated. Any commercial relationship relevant to a story is disclosed within that story, and sponsored content is always clearly labeled. Questions about the publication can be directed through our contact page.

---

# Editorial Standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/editorial-standards/

Editorial Standards
Komposite News reports facts we can verify and clearly distinguishes reporting from analysis and opinion. News stories describe what happened. Pieces labeled Analysis interpret events and draw conclusions from evidence. Pieces labeled Opinion argue a point of view and represent their author.
We attribute information to sources wherever possible, grant anonymity only when information is significant and cannot otherwise be obtained, and independently verify claims before publishing them. We do not accept payment for editorial coverage, and staff may not trade on non-public information obtained through reporting.
Sponsored or partner content, when it appears, is labeled unambiguously and is never presented in editorial form without that label. Errors, when they occur, are corrected promptly and transparently under our corrections policy.
How we use AI
Komposite News uses AI tools to help research, draft and edit stories. Every story is checked against the sources listed with it before publication, and quotes are published only when we can match them to a source or the person approved them. An editor approves each story before it goes live. Bylines name the desk or house byline responsible for a story; they are not always individual reporters. Corrections: contact the newsroom via our contact page with the article link and the specific claim at issue, as set out in our corrections policy.

# AI Policy

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai-policy/

AI Policy
Komposite News uses AI tools to help research, draft and edit stories, and to assist with translation and site infrastructure. AI is not a replacement for editorial judgment: every story is checked against the sources listed with it, and an editor approves each story before it goes live. Responsibility for accuracy rests with the newsroom, not with any tool used to produce it. Bylines name the desk or house byline responsible for a story; they are not always individual reporters. The full statement is in How we use AI.
Quotes are published only when we can match them to a source or the person approved them. We do not publish AI-generated statements attributed to real people, AI-fabricated data, or synthetic imagery presented as photography. Illustrations are labeled as illustrations, photographs carry credits and licenses, and sample or demonstration data is labeled as such wherever it appears.
This policy will evolve with the technology. Questions about how a specific story was produced can be directed to the newsroom via our contact page.

# What buyers actually do with an SBOM

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/sbom-what-buyers-do-with-it/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z

Software bills of materials are now routinely produced and routinely ignored, and the gap between generating one and acting on it is where the risk sits.

The argument about whether vendors should produce a software bill of materials is over. Vendors produce them. The interesting question, and the one procurement teams are least prepared for, is what happens to the file after it arrives.
An SBOM is an inventory: the components inside a piece of software, their versions, and their relationships to one another. Its value is entirely conditional. It answers one question well, which is whether a newly disclosed vulnerability is present in something already installed, and it answers that question only if somebody is holding it when the disclosure lands.
The baseline moved this year. American authorities published an updated set of minimum elements, replacing guidance that had stood since the original executive order and raising what a compliant document is expected to contain.
That update matters more than it sounds, because the minimum elements are what contracts point at. A purchase order rarely specifies a format in detail. It references a standard, and the standard quietly determines how much work a vendor has to do.
Adoption across the European market has been surveyed rather than assumed. The EU cybersecurity agency's review of where SBOM practice actually stands describes an ecosystem where generation is increasingly routine and consumption remains the weak link.
That asymmetry is the whole story. Producing an SBOM is a build-pipeline problem, and build pipelines are the part of software organizations most amenable to automation. Consuming one is an operations problem, and operations teams are already the most oversubscribed function in most security programs.
The result is a familiar organizational pattern. A file arrives, satisfies a contractual requirement, and is stored where nothing queries it. The obligation is met and the risk is unchanged, which is the worst of both outcomes because it also produces a record showing the buyer was told.
Teams that get value from the practice describe the same prerequisite, and it is not tooling. It is knowing what software they run, at which version, in which environment, well enough to join that list against an inventory. Organizations that cannot answer the first question gain nothing from the second.
Regulatory drivers keep expanding the population who must care. Medical device guidance, the European cyber resilience regime and federal procurement terms each require the artifact in their own context, and each has a different theory of what the recipient is supposed to do with it.
Practitioners are candid that the honest use case is narrower than the marketing. When a widely used component is found to be catastrophically vulnerable, an SBOM turns a week of frantic archaeology into a database query. Between those events it is a maintenance cost.
That is a reasonable trade and a smaller claim than the one usually made for it. The organizations doing this well are not the ones with the best-formatted files. They are the ones who can answer, on the afternoon the disclosure lands, where the affected component is running.

# What an attestation must prove

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/what-an-attestation-must-prove/
Section: Crypto
By: Marcus Oyelaran
Published: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z

Stablecoin law requires monthly examination of reserves, and the open rulemaking question is what level of assurance that examination must actually deliver.

The argument about whether stablecoin issuers should publish their reserves is finished. Federal law requires it. The argument that replaced it is narrower, more technical, and determines whether the requirement means very much: what an examination of those reserves has to establish.
The statute sets the frame. The GENIUS Act requires permitted issuers to publish the composition of their reserves monthly, to have those reports examined by a registered public accounting firm, and to obtain certifications from the chief executive and chief financial officer.
Monthly is a demanding cadence for anything an accounting firm signs. Most public company reporting is quarterly with a single annual audit, so the law is asking for a recurring procedure that has no exact precedent at this frequency.
The open question is the assurance level, and it is not a technicality. An examination performed at limited assurance concludes that nothing came to the practitioner's attention suggesting a problem. One performed at reasonable assurance states positively that the reserves are what the issuer says they are.
Those are different products with different costs and very different meanings to a reader, and the same document title can describe either. A holder comparing two issuers' monthly reports has no reliable way to tell which standard produced them without reading the fine print.
Regulators are consulting rather than assuming. Rulemaking has asked directly whether the examination should be conducted at reasonable assurance, under established attestation standards, or under an alternative framework built for the purpose.
The content of the disclosure is comparatively settled. The expected reporting covers the par value of coins outstanding, the fair value of reserve assets by category, the weighted average maturity of Treasury holdings, the names of custodians and depository institutions, and a reconciliation showing reserves at least equal outstanding coins.
That reconciliation is the heart of it. Everything else describes the portfolio; the reconciliation is the statement that the portfolio covers the liability, and it is the sentence a holder is actually relying on when they treat a token as a dollar.
Supervisors have published implementation requirements through the ordinary rulemaking process, including standards for insured depository institutions and supervised issuers, which is how a novel instrument gets absorbed into an existing supervisory apparatus.
The practical effect of a strong answer would be consolidation. A monthly reasonable-assurance examination is expensive, requires reserve assets an accounting firm can verify quickly, and is easiest for issuers holding short Treasuries at large custodians, which is a narrower field than the one that exists today.
That may be the intended outcome. A payment instrument that circulates as a dollar substitute is a poor place for structural creativity, and the assurance standard is the lever that decides how much of it survives.

# What a seed round now requires

URL: https://kompositenews.com/startups/what-a-seed-round-now-requires/
Section: Startups
By: Grace Lindqvist
Published: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z

Seed rounds now arrive after revenue and retention evidence that once belonged to Series A, and the gap between rounds has stretched past two years.

The seed round kept its name and quietly changed its meaning. What investors now expect before writing that check is roughly what a Series A required a few years ago, and founders planning against the old definition run out of money at the point they expected to raise.
The clearest expression of the shift is time. Data assembled from company cap tables shows the interval between rounds stretching well past two years, which means a seed round is no longer bridging to a nearby milestone. It has to fund the company to a materially different business.
That arithmetic changes how much to raise and what to promise. A round sized for eighteen months against a market that now takes twenty-four produces a company that is technically alive and practically unfundable, holding a deck full of progress and a bank balance that ends the conversation.
Investors describe the bar in terms of evidence rather than vision. Revenue that recurs, retention that survives a renewal cycle, and unit economics the founder can explain without a chart have replaced the narrative rounds that characterized the last cycle.
Pre-seed absorbed the difference. What used to be called seed is now a distinct earlier stage with its own norms and its own investors, which means the ladder gained a rung rather than losing one, and the founder climbs the same distance in more steps.
Formation costs falling has made this possible without making it pleasant. Building a credible product is cheaper than it has ever been, so the evidence investors demand is now genuinely obtainable before a round, which is precisely why it is demanded.
The concentration of capital into a narrow band of companies compounds the effect. When most of a fund's deployment goes to a small number of category-defining bets, the diligence applied to everything else tightens, because those checks have to clear a higher internal bar to justify the attention.
Founders who have raised recently describe the practical adaptation as unglamorous. Charge earlier than feels comfortable, treat the first ten paying customers as the fundraise rather than as a precursor to it, and keep the burn low enough that the round is optional for a quarter longer than planned.
The uncomfortable part is what this selects for. Requiring commercial evidence before capital favors founders who can survive unpaid for longer, which is a filter on personal circumstances as much as on ability, and the industry has not found a good answer to that.
Investors are candid that the discipline is real and its distribution is not. The companies that clear the new bar are unquestionably stronger at the same stage than their predecessors, and some number of good companies never got far enough to be measured.
The stage will keep its name regardless. It is worth understanding that the word now describes a company with customers, and planning the eighteen months before it accordingly.

# AI in the order flow: what machine trading is doing to volatility

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/volatility-market-structure-ai-trading/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z

Adaptive execution and model-driven strategies are changing intraday dynamics in ways researchers are only beginning to measure.

Machine learning has been in markets for years, but the current generation of adaptive execution and model-driven strategies behaves differently from its rule-based ancestors, and researchers are working out what that means for volatility itself.
Early findings are mixed in instructive ways. Adaptive strategies appear to dampen volatility in normal conditions, adjusting quickly to absorb flow imbalances, while contributing to sharper moves when many models respond to the same signal simultaneously. Calm most days, and a faster crowd on the days that matter.
Regulators are asking measurement questions before policy ones: how much flow is model-driven, how correlated are the models, and whether existing circuit breakers match the speed of the herding they are meant to interrupt. Exchanges, holding the data, have become reluctant referees in the debate.
RelatedDigital asset market making becomes an institutional business ›Practitioners mostly shrug at the framing. Every generation of market technology, they note, was accused of breaking volatility until it became the baseline against which the next generation was accused. The honest answer is that the market is running the experiment on itself, and the results publish in real time.

# Machine identity sprawl becomes security's biggest inventory problem

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/identity-machine-workloads/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z

Service accounts, API keys, and agent credentials now outnumber human identities many times over, and governance is racing the growth.

For every human identity in a modern enterprise there are many machine ones, service accounts, API keys, certificates, and now AI agent credentials, and most organizations cannot count them, let alone govern them. Machine identity has become the inventory problem that defines the next phase of identity security.
The risk profile is distinctive: machine credentials are long-lived, widely copied, and rarely owned by anyone who remembers creating them. Incident reviews repeatedly trace breaches to forgotten service accounts with standing privileges, and the remediation is lifecycle discipline, issuance, rotation, expiry, applied at a scale human identity never required.
RelatedCybersecurity spending shifts toward identity and resilience ›Agentic AI raised the stakes by adding credentials that act autonomously. The emerging standard treats every agent as a governed identity with scoped permissions and an accountable human sponsor, which is less a new idea than the old one, finally enforced on the population that grew fastest.

# Enterprises write the rulebook for AI-generated code

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-coding-tools-enterprise-standards/
Section: AI
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z
Updated: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z

Provenance tracking, review gates, and dependency policies are turning AI coding assistance from a developer perk into governed infrastructure.

AI coding assistants arrived in enterprises through developer enthusiasm and settled in ahead of policy. The policy is now catching up. Engineering organizations are formalizing rules for machine-generated code: what must be tracked, what must be reviewed differently, and what may not be generated at all.
Provenance is the anchor requirement. Compliance teams want to know which code a model wrote, which model wrote it, and what the model was shown, both for license exposure and for the audits that regulated industries already face. Tooling vendors have responded with attribution tracking that engineering leaders describe as necessary and nobody describes as finished.
RelatedAI infrastructure spending moves into a new phase ›The practical effect on productivity has been smaller than skeptics predicted. Teams report that governance slowed adoption for a quarter and then became routine, the same arc that source control and code review followed in earlier decades. The tools stayed; the anarchy did not.

# AI evaluation grows from afterthought to budget line

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-evaluation-becomes-budget-line/
Section: AI
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z

Enterprises deploying models at scale are formalizing evaluation the way they once formalized QA, and a vendor category is forming around it.

When AI systems were pilots, evaluation was a spreadsheet. Now that they process claims, answer customers, and draft contracts, companies are treating evaluation as standing infrastructure, with dedicated staff, tooling budgets, and sign-off authority over releases.
The change is driven less by regulation than by incident reports. Organizations that shipped model updates without regression testing describe the same experience: a quiet degradation in some workflow no one was watching, discovered by customers rather than dashboards. Formal evaluation pipelines are the institutional response.
A market is forming to serve the need. Startups sell evaluation harnesses, scored datasets tailored to industries, and monitoring that flags drift in production. Incumbent observability vendors are extending into the category, arguing that model behavior is simply another production signal.
RelatedEnterprise buyers push for clearer AI contract terms ›The maturity marker executives cite is procedural: whether a model change can be blocked. In organizations where evaluation owns a veto, the function is real. Where it produces reports no one must read, it remains a spreadsheet with a bigger budget.

# Power availability becomes the master constraint on computing

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/power-constraints-shape-computing/
Section: Technology
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z

Grid interconnection queues, not chip supply, now set the timeline for new capacity, and the industry is reorganizing around electrons.

Ask data center developers what gates their next project and the answer is no longer silicon. It is the interconnection queue, the multi-year wait for utility approval to draw large amounts of power from grids that were not planned for computing's growth curve.
The constraint is reorganizing the industry's geography and structure. Development migrates to regions with spare generation and faster approvals; operators contract directly for new generation, sometimes co-developing it; and a market has emerged in sites whose chief asset is a signed interconnection agreement.
On-site and adjacent generation has moved from contingency to strategy. Gas turbines as bridge power, long-term contracts anchoring new renewable buildouts, and serious capital behind small modular nuclear all reflect the same conclusion: waiting for the grid is the expensive option.
RelatedLiquid cooling stops being optional in AI data centers ›The policy dimension is unavoidable. Computing's power demand lands on ratepayers, regulators, and climate commitments simultaneously, and jurisdictions are diverging on who pays for the upgrades and who gets priority in the queue. Where those questions get answered favorably is, increasingly, where the next generation of infrastructure gets built.

# Shadow AI becomes the new shadow IT

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/shadow-ai-governance-problem/
Section: Business
By: Sam Porter
Published: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z

Employees are routing work through unsanctioned AI tools faster than policies can name them, and enterprises are choosing between control and visibility.

Every technology wave produces its shadow, and AI's arrived on schedule. Employees across functions are routing drafting, analysis, and coding through personal accounts on consumer AI tools, outside procurement, outside logging, and outside whatever policy the company wrote last quarter.
The governance instinct is prohibition, and the operational evidence is that prohibition fails quietly. Organizations that blocked consumer tools report usage migrating to personal devices, trading visible risk for invisible risk. The emerging alternative is substitution: sanctioned tools good enough that the shadow versions lose their appeal, paired with monitoring that treats AI traffic like any other data flow.
RelatedEnterprise software pricing strains under the weight of AI ›Security leaders describe the moment in familiar terms, because they lived it with cloud storage and messaging apps. The lesson they cite from those episodes is consistent: the workforce adopts what works, and governance succeeds by arriving with a better answer rather than a longer denial.

# Instant payments become table stakes in B2B

URL: https://kompositenews.com/fintech/instant-payments-b2b-standard/
Section: Fintech
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z

Real-time rails are moving from consumer novelty to supplier expectation, and the software layer on top is where the margin lives.

Instant payment rails, built for consumers splitting dinner, are being colonized by business finance. Supplier payments, insurance disbursements, and payroll adjustments increasingly ride real-time systems, and the expectation is spreading through supply chains faster than the infrastructure teams behind it anticipated.
The shift exposes where the value actually sits. Moving money instantly is becoming a commodity; knowing why it moved is not. The software that attaches invoices, remittance data, and reconciliation to real-time payments commands the margin the rails themselves are losing.
Corporate adoption follows a practical script: start with the payments where speed is worth money, urgent supplier releases, claim payouts, final payrolls, then expand as finance teams trust the controls. Fraud tooling has had to accelerate in parallel, since irrevocable and instant is a demanding combination.
RelatedWhen software spends: payments build an authorization layer for AI agents ›Banks find themselves both essential and squeezed, operating the rails while fintech intermediaries own the customer experience above them. The competitive response, embedding payment capabilities directly into the software businesses already use, is reshaping bank product organizations around a fact they long resisted: the interface is the relationship.

# Stablecoin Reserve reporting converges on common standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-standards/
Section: Crypto
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z
Updated: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z

Monthly attestations are giving way to standardized disclosures that let treasurers compare issuers the way they compare money market funds.

Stablecoin issuers are learning to speak the language of money market funds. Reserve disclosures, once a patchwork of voluntary attestations in incompatible formats, are converging on standardized reporting of composition, maturity, and counterparties, driven by regulation in some jurisdictions and competitive pressure everywhere else.
The audience is corporate. Treasurers evaluating stablecoins for payments want the same visibility they get from a fund fact sheet, and issuers courting that demand have discovered that transparency is a product feature. Disclosure quality now appears in payment providers' issuer scorecards alongside redemption terms.
Standardization enables comparison, and comparison disciplines behavior. Analysts publishing side-by-side reserve breakdowns note measurable shifts toward shorter maturities and simpler holdings since standard formats took hold, the market rewarding conservatism it can finally see.
RelatedStablecoin law meets its implementation year ›Gaps remain, particularly in real-time reporting and the treatment of reserves held across borders. But the direction is set, and it points toward stablecoins being evaluated with the tools of cash management rather than the vocabulary of crypto.

# Interoperability standards take shape for institutional chains

URL: https://kompositenews.com/blockchain/interoperability-standards-institutional-chains/
Section: Blockchain
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z
Updated: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z

Messaging standards bodies and blockchain consortia are converging on formats that let regulated ledgers talk to each other, and to the systems banks already run.

The institutional blockchain world is discovering what payments learned decades ago: networks that cannot interoperate stay small. Standards work, unfashionable and slow, has become the venue where the next phase of adoption is actually being decided.
The convergence underway joins two traditions. Financial messaging bodies bring the discipline of standardized data formats that banks already parse, while blockchain consortia bring transfer protocols proven on public networks. The emerging designs let a tokenized asset move between regulated ledgers while carrying the structured information compliance systems require.
Progress is measured in pilots that would once have been impossible: assets issued on one institution's ledger settling against payment on another's, with both sides reconciled automatically. Participants emphasize that none of it required the institutions to share a chain, only a vocabulary.
RelatedBanks test blockchain settlement without abandoning existing rails ›The stakes are consolidation versus fragmentation. If common standards hold, tokenized markets can scale across institutions the way correspondent banking did. If they fail, each network remains an island, and the efficiency case for the technology weakens accordingly.

# Forty-one billion raised, nine billion short

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/forty-one-billion-raised-nine-billion-short/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-10-29T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-29T14:00:00Z

Alphabet's free cash flow was minus $9.1bn in Q3 as capex hit $51.4bn; it raised $41.1bn in debt and stock. Microsoft's stayed positive at $18.6bn.

Alphabet's free cash flow was minus $9.1bn in the third quarter after it spent $51.4bn on property and equipment, a gap it covered with $28.7bn of bonds and $12.4bn of new shares, its results release on Wednesday shows. Microsoft, reporting the same evening, doubled its own spending and still generated $18.6bn of free cash.
Alphabet's revenue rose 25 per cent to $127.6bn in the three months to 30 September. Operating cash flow fell to $42.3bn from $48.4bn a year earlier, while purchases of property and equipment rose to $51.4bn from $24.0bn. The company made no share buybacks in the quarter, against $11.5bn a year earlier, and paid $2.9bn in dividends. It issued $28.7bn of senior unsecured notes and sold 12m Class A and 24m Class C shares through an at-the-market programme for $12.4bn, with $27.6bn of that programme still available at the end of September. Long-term debt stood at $125.1bn, up from $46.5bn at the end of 2025.
It is the second quarter running in which Alphabet has spent more than it generated. Free cash flow was minus $5.9bn in the second quarter, the first negative quarter since the company listed in 2004, InvestingCube reported at the time. On the release's own measure, trailing twelve-month free cash flow has fallen to $19.7bn. The company kept its 2026 capital spending forecast at $195bn to $205bn and said spending in 2027 will "increase significantly", The Motley Fool reported.

Sources: Alphabet's third-quarter release and Microsoft's first-quarter release, 28 October 2026, cash flow statements for the three months to 30 September. Free cash flow and ratios are Komposite's arithmetic (operating cash flow less purchases of property and equipment).Microsoft's numbers show the other way to pay for the same thing. Its fiscal first-quarter release shows revenue up 19 per cent to $92.3bn, Azure cloud revenue up 48 per cent and additions to property and equipment of $39.4bn, up from $19.4bn. Operating cash flow rose to $58.0bn, so free cash flow, by our arithmetic, was $18.6bn, down 27 per cent from $25.7bn a year earlier but positive. Microsoft issued no debt, repaid $4.9bn and bought back $4.4bn of its shares. Including finance leases, its capital spending was $45.2bn, The Motley Fool reported.
"We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate," Sundar Pichai, Alphabet's chief executive, said in the release. Investors read it differently. Alphabet's shares were down 10.3 per cent at $291.50 before the open on Thursday, Investing.com reported, and were down about 13 per cent later in the session, putting the stock on course for its worst day since its 2004 listing and nearly $500bn of market value at stake, Yahoo Finance reported. Microsoft "held up better", Yahoo said, and the Nasdaq Composite fell more than 1 per cent.
The earnings line was weaker too. Diluted earnings per share fell to $2.12 from $2.87, against an analyst consensus of roughly $3.02 cited by Investing.com, partly because of an $8.7bn loss on equity securities, which Investing.com attributed mainly to Alphabet's stake in SpaceX. Google Cloud was the exception: revenue rose 103 per cent to $30.7bn and operating income to $11.1bn. Brent Thill, an analyst at Jefferies, said cloud was "the only business that beat" and "everything else missed", according to Investing.com.
The share sales came at higher prices than Thursday's. By our arithmetic, Alphabet's at-the-market sales raised an average of roughly $358 for each Class A share and $338 for each Class C share, net of costs, against $291.50 before Thursday's open. A year earlier, Alphabet was spending $11.5bn a quarter buying its shares back; in the third quarter it was a net seller. Capital spending equal to 121 per cent of operating cash flow, against 68 per cent at Microsoft, is the gap the market priced on Thursday.
Why it matters: the largest AI builders are now splitting into those that can fund data centres from operations and those that need the capital markets. Meta priced $37.5bn of new equity on Monday after its own free cash flow turned negative, Komposite reported, and Apollo's chief economist has argued that the financial payoff from AI stops at seven companies. Alphabet's cloud business, which is now renting its chips through Oracle, is the part of the company growing fast enough to justify the spending; the question its shareholders asked on Thursday is how long the rest has to pay for it.

# Google's chips go to work in Oracle's cloud

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/googles-chips-go-to-work-in-oracles-cloud/
Section: AI
By: Dana Whitfield
Published: 2026-10-29T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-29T13:40:00Z

Oracle will rent out Google's TPU AI chips in its cloud from 2027, and OpenAI reportedly plans to buy them, as Google's chips move beyond Google Cloud.

Oracle will offer Google's tensor processing units, the custom AI chips Google designs for its own data centres, to customers of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027, the company said on Tuesday at its AI World conference in Las Vegas. Oracle says that makes it the first hyperscale cloud outside Google's own to offer the chips, The Register reported.
The chips will be selectable in Oracle's cloud from 2027, with capacity growing over several years, but Oracle did not say how many it will deploy. Oracle will house them in its own data centres and supply the power, cooling and networking, TNW reported. Google's eighth generation comes in two versions, the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference; Google says the 8t delivers nearly three times the compute per pod of its predecessor. Karan Batta, a senior vice-president at Oracle's cloud unit, described a "multi-year, multi-gigawatt partnership", according to TNW's account of his remarks to DatacenterDynamics.
"Different AI workloads have different compute needs," Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, said in the announcement, as quoted by The Register. "Bringing Google TPUs to OCI gives customers ... the flexibility to choose the right infrastructure," he added. Oracle announced on the same day that Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 systems were generally available in its cloud, and it has Nvidia commitments The Register put at "tens of billions" of dollars, so the TPUs arrive as an addition rather than a replacement.
The second report is less firm. The Information reported on Tuesday that OpenAI plans to buy Google's TPUs, citing one person familiar with the matter, and gave no price, volume or timing. OpenAI declined to comment to Reuters and Google did not immediately respond, TNW said; Komposite has not been able to confirm the report. OpenAI is one of the largest buyers of Nvidia's processors, and unveiled its first custom chip, designed with Broadcom, in June.
WhenWhoWhatStatus
June 2025OpenAIBegan renting Google's TPUsReported by Reuters; OpenAI then said it had no active plans to use them in its products
April 2026GoogleSaid it would sell TPU hardware directly to a small group of customers to run in their own data centresCompany statement
By September 2026Anthropic5GW of Google TPU capacity coming through BroadcomAnnounced; reported by Komposite on 18 September

27 October 2026OpenAIPlans to buy Google's TPUsReported by The Information from one source; not confirmed
Sources: TNW, TNW, The Register and Komposite's earlier reporting. Timeline compiled by Komposite.The pattern is a chip that used to stay at home. Google said in April that it would sell TPU hardware directly to a small group of customers who could run it in their own data centres, and Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet's chief financial officer, has said she expects a small share of TPU sales revenue to be booked this year with most of it in 2027, according to TNW. Demand from customers including Anthropic, which has 5GW of Google TPU capacity coming through Broadcom, has been strong enough that Google's own researchers have had to wait for access, TNW reported.
It is also showing in Google's numbers. Alphabet's third-quarter results, published on Wednesday, show Google Cloud revenue up 103 per cent to $30.7bn, "powered by huge demand for our AI infrastructure and AI solutions", and cloud operating income of $11.1bn. By our arithmetic, that is an operating margin of 36 per cent, against 24 per cent a year earlier. The same results showed Alphabet spending more on data centres than it took in from operations, which is the subject of Komposite's lead story today.
Why it matters: Nvidia's position in AI computing rests partly on the fact that its chips can be rented from all the large clouds, while Google's could be rented mainly from Google. Oracle's deal and, if confirmed, an OpenAI purchase would make TPUs a second chip that can be bought or rented outside the company that designs it. Oracle's shares rose nearly 5 per cent on Tuesday, TNW reported, citing CNBC, but are down more than 30 per cent this year on investor concern about how it will pay for its data centres. The Register's Brandon Vigliarolo called much of the week's news "circular spending" among the largest AI companies.
OpenAI has been widening its suppliers for months: it was seeking thirty billion dollars of new funding this month, Komposite reported, and the chip start-up Tenstorrent more than doubled its valuation on the same demand for alternatives to Nvidia.

# Twenty-five thousand posts, and no number for AI

URL: https://kompositenews.com/policy/twenty-five-thousand-posts-and-no-number-for-ai/
Section: Policy
By: Jonathan Bright
Published: 2026-10-29T13:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-29T13:20:00Z

The Netherlands plans to cut 25,000 civil-service posts by 2035 to save €3.5bn a year, but its letter says not to overestimate AI and gives it no number.

The Dutch government plans to cut about 25,000 full-time posts from its central civil service by 2035, but the letter announcing it on Monday puts no figure on how many jobs artificial intelligence will replace. State Secretary Eric van der Burg sent it to parliament. The cut, about one post in six, is meant to save €900m in 2027, rising to €3.5bn a year from 2035, the public broadcaster NOS reported.
The letter, a progress report on the cabinet's "Slagvaardige Overheid" (effective government) programme sent to the lower house on 26 October, counts 160,016 full-time equivalents in central government and calls the 25,000 figure a rough estimate, according to AI Insider, a Dutch trade site that published extracts. Police and Defence are exempt, as are the prison service, the Public Prosecution Service and the security services. The benefits agency UWV, the immigration service IND and the tax administration were not exempted in advance, NOS said. Many organisations face cuts of about 20 per cent, some about 45 per cent and one about 60 per cent.
The international framing was simpler. Bloomberg described an "AI-led efficiency drive" and quoted Mr van der Burg: "We cannot keep doing what we have been doing," and the goal is a central government that is "simpler, smarter, and smaller". Bloomberg also reported that parliament had passed non-binding motions calling for a 20 per cent productivity increase through AI, and that the cabinet would present plans for deploying the technology early next year.
The letter is more cautious than the headlines. "Overschat de formatieve effecten van digitalisering en AI niet," it says, as quoted by AI Insider: do not overestimate the staffing effects of digitalisation and AI. It sets no AI target until the first quarter of 2027, when the house has asked for one, and says security, data quality and sovereignty must be in order, infrastructure adapted and work processes fundamentally revised first. Earlier rounds of digitisation, it notes, did not deliver the promised lower costs and smaller staff; they produced new tasks, more capacity and more hired-in workers.
PointWhat the letter saysHow it was widely reported
Size of the cutAbout 25,000 fte of 160,016, which Mr van der Burg calls a rough estimate25,000 jobs
Role of AI"Do not overestimate" the staffing effects of digitalisation and AI; no AI figure until the first quarter of 2027An "AI-led" overhaul
Where the savings come fromGeneral efficiency of at most 0.5 per cent a year covers about a third; the rest from dropping tasksAI productivity gains
Who is sparedPolice and Defence, the prison service, the Public Prosecution Service and the security servicesPolice and the military
Money&euro;900m in 2027, rising to &euro;3.5bn a year from 2035&euro;3.5bn a year
Sources: AI Insider's reading of the letter, NOS and Bloomberg. Comparison compiled by Komposite.Most of the saving is meant to come from doing less. AI Insider reports that general efficiency of at most 0.5 per cent a year, the figure used by the CPB, the government's economic forecaster, covers about a third of the target, and that the remainder must come from dropping tasks. By our arithmetic, 0.5 per cent a year compounded over the nine years from 2027 to 2035 comes to about 4.4 per cent of 160,016, or roughly 7,100 posts, a little short of a third of 25,000 (about 8,300). NOS lists the measures as leaner facilities at ministries, standardised IT systems and efficiency measures "including with AI", plus cuts to 28 advisory councils and about 150 advisory committees.
The baseline has moved the other way for years. Central government grew by about 41 per cent, or 46,500 full-time equivalents, between 2018 and 2025, according to the letter as AI Insider reports it, and Bloomberg put the number of officials at a record 160,000 at the end of last year. By our subtraction, a cut of 25,000 would leave about 135,000 posts, still roughly 21,500 more than in 2018. The €3.5bn target works out at about €140,000 a year for each post removed, by our arithmetic, which suggests the figure covers more than salaries alone.
Why it matters: governments are starting to book AI into budgets before they have measured it. The Dutch plan fixes the saving now and leaves the AI contribution to a later document, which means the technology's share will be judged against a target already set. Parliament's 20 per cent productivity motion and the letter's own caution now point in different directions, and the first-quarter AI plan will have to reconcile them. Mr van der Burg said he hoped to complete much of the detail within six months, NOS reported; the precise allocation is due in the spring budget memorandum, according to the letter as AI Insider reports it.
The Dutch state has moved carefully on technology before: its tax administration said this month it would run its mail on its own servers rather than finish a move to Microsoft 365, Komposite reported. In the United States, the federal government has taken the procurement route, ordering DeepSeek out of civilian agencies, while in the private sector Microsoft has offered buyouts to about 60,000 staff as it raises AI spending.

# Thirty-seven and a half billion, with sixty to follow

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/thirty-seven-and-a-half-billion-with-sixty-to-follow/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-10-28T23:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-28T23:40:00Z

Meta priced $25bn of stock at $625 and $12.5bn of convertible preferred, and plans a $60bn share programme in 2027 as AI spending outruns its cash flow.

Meta Platforms priced $37.5bn of new equity late on Monday, selling $25bn of Class A common stock at $625 a share and $12.5bn of mandatory convertible preferred stock, the company said in its pricing announcement. It also said it plans to sell about $60bn more stock through an at-the-market programme from next year.
The common stock sale was upsized to $25.0bn from $22.5bn and is structured as a forward sale. Affiliates of Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, the two lead bookrunners, will borrow and sell 40m Class A shares now; Meta will deliver new shares and collect about $24.9bn, at an initial forward price of about $622.92, on dates of its choosing on or before 19 November 2027. Meta expects no proceeds from that initial sale of borrowed shares, the release said. The preferred stock is sold as 250m depositary shares at $50, each a twentieth of a share carrying a 6.50 per cent annual dividend, and converts into Class A stock around 15 August 2029. Both offerings are expected to close on Thursday, and the proceeds are for "general corporate purposes".
The third piece is not yet a deal. In a free writing prospectus filed with the SEC, Meta said it "plans to launch an approximately $60 billion at-the-market ('ATM') program" once its new non-voting Class C shares begin trading, and that the programme "is not expected to commence until the first quarter of 2027". It added that it "has not entered into any agreement" and that "the timing, size and terms of any such program, if established, have not been determined." An at-the-market programme lets a company sell shares into the market in small amounts over time rather than in one underwritten block.
PieceSizeTermsStatus
Class A common stock, forward sale$25.0bn (40m shares at $625); up to $3.75bn moreMorgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs affiliates sell borrowed shares now; Meta delivers shares and takes about $24.9bn on or before 19 Nov 2027Priced 26 Oct; closes 29 Oct
Mandatory convertible preferred (depositary shares)$12.5bn (250m at $50); up to 37.5m more6.50% dividend; converts around 15 Aug 2029 into 0.0681 to 0.0800 Class A shares per depositary sharePriced 26 Oct; closes 29 Oct
At-the-market programme, Class C stockAbout $60bnSold from time to time through a manager; no agreement signed; timing, size and terms not determinedNot before the first quarter of 2027
Total$37.5bn priced; $97.5bn including the planned programmeOur arithmetic, before over-allotment options
Sources: Meta's pricing announcement, free writing prospectus and prospectus supplement, all 26 October 2026. Totals are Komposite's arithmetic.Three chipmakers are on the buy side. The prospectus supplement names NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom as "Cornerstone Investors" that "indicated an interest in purchasing up to an aggregate of $5.0 billion" of the common stock, about a fifth of the offering by our arithmetic, and says the indications are "not binding agreements or commitments to purchase". The Motley Fool reported that Nvidia said it would invest $3bn; Komposite has not seen that figure in a filing. The price of $625 was about 0.9 per cent below the last sale of $630.56 on Monday, by our arithmetic from that report, and the shares closed at $612.49 on Wednesday, down 1.24 per cent.
The reason is in the cash flow statement. Meta's third-quarter results, published on 21 October, show capital expenditure, including finance-lease principal, of $34.91bn in the quarter and free cash flow of minus $2.12bn. The company kept its 2026 capital spending forecast at $135bn to $145bn and made no share buybacks in the quarter. It ended September with $82.45bn of cash and marketable securities, and the preliminary prospectus puts total consolidated indebtedness at $83.7bn. Investing.com described the negative free cash flow as the first in more than a decade.
The dilution is modest on its own. By our arithmetic, the 40m new common shares equal 1.6 per cent of the 2,556m Class A and Class B shares outstanding on 30 September, and the preferred will convert into between 17.0m and 20.0m more, so the two priced deals add 2.2 to 2.3 per cent before over-allotment options, or up to 2.7 per cent if both are exercised in full. The full $60bn programme, at Monday's price, would be roughly another 3.8 per cent. At $625 a share, the $37.5bn priced is about 2.3 per cent of Meta's market value of roughly $1.6tn. The preferred dividend costs about $812.5m a year.
The order of the deals matters for control. Meta created the Class C shares, which carry no votes, so that it could raise equity without diluting Mark Zuckerberg, who held about 60.6 per cent of the voting power, as Komposite reported last week. Monday's sale, however, is of voting Class A shares, because the Class C stock does not take effect until 19 January. By our arithmetic from the prospectus share counts, 40m new Class A votes take Mr Zuckerberg's share to about 60.2 per cent, and conversion of the preferred into Class A would take it to about 59.9 per cent. The filings allow the forward sales and the preferred to be settled in Class C stock in some circumstances, which would avoid that.
Why it matters: Meta has paid for its data centres from operating cash and, increasingly, from bonds; The Motley Fool counts $29.9bn of long-term borrowing in the fourth quarter of 2025 and $24.9bn in the second quarter of 2026. It is now adding equity, with chipmakers among the would-be buyers. Against the midpoint of its 2026 spending forecast, the $37.5bn priced this week would cover about 27 per cent of a single year's capital expenditure, by our arithmetic, and the cash from the common stock is not due until as late as November 2027.
Other capital-intensive AI builders have reached for different structures. SpaceX took $40bn of GPU financing as a lease from an Apollo-managed vehicle, Komposite reported on Monday, and Apollo's chief economist argued at the weekend that the financial payoff from AI has so far stopped at seven companies, Meta among them. Meta has now asked public shareholders to fund more of the bet directly.

# AI gets the law wrong. A podcast bets on chapters

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/ai-gets-the-law-wrong-a-podcast-bets-on-chapters/
Section: Technology
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-10-28T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-28T15:00:00Z

AI assistants still garble legal detail. Two Taps and Friends, a defense lawyers' podcast, uses chapters, transcripts and clip markup to be found instead.

Studies keep finding that AI assistants get legal and news detail wrong, and one podcast hosted by criminal defense lawyers is answering with metadata. Two Taps and Friends marks up its episodes with chapters, transcripts and clip data so that search engines point people to the lawyers' explanation itself.
The accuracy problem is well documented. Researchers writing for Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI reported hallucination rates of 69% to 88% when they put specific legal queries to GPT 3.5, Llama 2 and PaLM 2, in a study published in January 2024. Those models have since been replaced, but the pattern has carried into news. A study of more than 3,000 answers from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity, coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union and led by the BBC, found that "45% of all AI answers had at least one significant issue", VRT reported in October 2025. In criminal law the detail that gets dropped is often the one that matters: whether a charge came by information or by indictment, or whether a federal count was dismissed rather than tried.
Two Taps and Friends is a weekly show on YouTube and the podcast apps. Daniel Rosenberg, who runs a criminal defense practice in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, hosts it with fellow defense attorneys Michael Dye and Lloyd Golburgh. Its Legal Panel episodes explain trials "the way working defense lawyers see them", the show's site says.
Komposite analysis: how one episode is packaged for machines. We counted the layers the show publishes around its audio, using its public catalogue, its episode pages and its podcast host.
LayerWhat the show publishesWhat a machine can read
Chapters95 of 98 catalogue entries, 1,338 markers, a median of 14 an episodeTimestamped titles, often naming the legal rule at issue
Clip markupEpisode 94's page lists its 16 chapters as schema.org Clip objectsStart and end times a search engine can link to directly
TranscriptsFull text on the Buzzsprout pages for episodes 84 and 94The lawyers' exact words, quotable and searchable
Written explainers114 Two Taps News stories that link back to episodesA crawlable article for each case
Clips and Shorts925 listed in the catalogueShort entry points that lead back to the full episode
Google says creators can steer this. Its video guidance states: "We will prioritize key moments set by you, either through structured data or the YouTube description." Two Taps titles many of its chapters after the rule in dispute rather than the headline. On episode 94, about the search of Representative Ilhan Omar's home, the chapters cover probable cause, how far a warrant for phones reaches and grand jury subpoenas. On episode 84, about Luigi Mangione, they cover state versus federal charges and New York's double jeopardy rule. Someone searching for either rule can land on the minute where a lawyer explains it.
The transcripts carry the reasoning verbatim. "Now, what I will say is to get a search warrant is not so easy, right?" Rosenberg says in the episode 94 transcript. "The standard is not the same as of a conviction. Conviction is beyond a reasonable doubt. The standard is probable cause for a search warrant, right?"
Clips are the risky layer. A 60-second cut can reach people who will never sit through 48 minutes, and it can also lose the caveat. The chapters and transcripts work as the backstop, because each clip points back to a full episode where the argument is on the record. "People search for a case, not for a podcast. When someone looks up a trial, we want a defense lawyer's explanation to be what they find," Rosenberg said. "A headline can tell you someone was charged. It can't tell you whether the charge was brought the right way, and that is often where a case is won or lost," he added.
The audience is there to be found. YouTube said in February 2025 that it had more than 1 billion monthly active viewers of podcast content. Rosenberg ends episodes with the creator's usual request to subscribe, because "it builds the channel, helps us more outreach, get more topics, get more guests". The show says nothing on it is legal advice. New full episodes usually arrive on Wednesdays, the show says, on its YouTube channel.
Komposite has reported on companies paying to be named in AI search answers, and on agencies that build channels while the platforms still own the field.
This feature was prepared in cooperation with Two Taps & Friends.

# A hundred trillion won, and short until 2030

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/a-hundred-trillion-won-and-short-until-2030/
Section: Technology
By: Tom Kessler
Published: 2026-10-28T13:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-28T13:20:00Z

SK hynix posted record Q3 revenue of ₩104.6tn and an 80% operating margin, and said memory demand will outrun supply through 2030.

SK hynix, the South Korean memory maker, reported record third-quarter revenue of ₩104.6tn on Wednesday, its first quarter above ₩100tn, and said demand for memory chips would exceed supply through 2030, according to its results release.
The release gives revenue of ₩104,615.5bn for the three months to September, up 32 per cent on the second quarter and 328 per cent on a year earlier. Operating profit was ₩83,333.8bn, up 38 per cent on the quarter and 632 per cent on the year, for an operating margin of 80 per cent, against 76 per cent in the second quarter and 47 per cent a year ago. Net income was ₩39,775.6bn, a net margin of 38 per cent. The figures are preliminary and prepared under Korean IFRS, the company said.
Net income fell 58 per cent from the second quarter, when it was ₩93,922.6bn, even as operating profit rose. By our subtraction, second-quarter net income exceeded operating profit by ₩33.4tn, while third-quarter net income was ₩43.6tn below it. The results release does not explain either gap; on the operating line, every measure rose.
QuarterRevenue (₩bn)Operating profit (₩bn)Operating marginNet income (₩bn)
Q3 202524,448.911,383.447%12,597.5
Q2 202679,318.760,542.676%93,922.6
Q3 2026104,615.583,333.880%39,775.6
Source: SK hynix results release, 28 October 2026; preliminary, K-IFRS. Margins are the company's, checked by our arithmetic (83,333.8 / 104,615.5 = 79.7 per cent).The outlook is the part customers will read most closely. The company said it "expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030", citing the technical difficulty of new products and the long lead times for new fabrication plants. It has signed long-term agreements (LTAs), contracts that commit volumes for several years, with 14 major customers including global cloud providers. The release says the volume secured so far corresponds to "more than 50% of total production capacity for 2027 and 2028"; the contracts typically run five years and use a price range that moves with market conditions, and some customers are discussing extensions.
On products, SK hynix said server DDR5 and the start of HBM4 shipments drove DRAM sales. HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is stacked DRAM packaged next to AI accelerators. The company expects HBM4 to pass the previous generation, HBM3E, in both shipments and revenue in the fourth quarter, and said its M15X fab will reach full capacity by the end of the year, with the first phase of its Yongin cluster entering full operation next year. It gave no capital expenditure figure, saying only that infrastructure investment will rise significantly and that it will adjust its scale and timing flexibly.
The cash is going back to shareholders at a pace that matches the margins. The company has a 2026 target of about ₩100tn in total returns, including at least ₩30tn of dividends and at least ₩60tn of buybacks and cancellations. It declared a third-quarter dividend of ₩20,000 a share, about ₩14tn in total, half of it a special dividend sharing gains from its investment in Kioxia, and a ₩20tn buyback, of which about ₩10tn will fund employee compensation and is excluded from the returns total. Net cash stood at ₩98.7tn at the end of September: ₩114.5tn of cash against ₩15.8tn of borrowings. The company also said it had stopped reviewing an initial public offering of its Solidigm subsidiary. "The IPO was intended to raise external capital for the expansion of Solidigm's production facilities," said Kwak Noh-Jung, the chief executive.
What the release says and how it was reported part in one place. The Register reported operating profit of ₩87.68tn, up 486 per cent on a year earlier. The company's own table gives ₩83,333.8bn and 632 per cent, and its numbers are internally consistent: ₩11,383.4bn a year earlier multiplied by 7.32 gives the third-quarter figure, by our arithmetic. We use the company's figures. The Register also reported that Kim Woo-hyun, the chief financial officer, said PC and mobile shipment volumes "are expected to decrease", a remark not in the release, and that the shares rose about 3 per cent in after-hours trading.
For scale, Samsung Electronics guided on 8 October to about ₩107.4tn of third-quarter operating profit on about ₩195tn of sales across all of its businesses, a margin of about 55 per cent by our arithmetic. SK hynix, which makes only memory, earned nearly four-fifths as much operating profit on a little over half the sales.
Why it matters: the shortage statement is a supplier's forecast, and a supplier has reason to describe its market as tight while it negotiates five-year contracts. But it is backed by contracts rather than adjectives: more than half of two years of future capacity has been committed to 14 buyers before some of the plants that will produce it are finished. For the cloud companies building AI data centres, memory is being priced in advance and in ranges; for PC and phone makers outside those agreements, it means competing for what is left.
The figures extend a pattern Komposite has tracked across the memory industry. In September we reported that Micron's gross margin had reached 84.6 per cent on almost flat bit shipments, with customers paying deposits in advance. Korea's export-credit researchers have put the data centre AI chip market at $860bn by 2030, the same year SK hynix now gives for the end of the shortage.

# Jio lists a fifth higher, on three per cent of its shares

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/jio-lists-a-fifth-higher-on-three-per-cent-of-its-shares/
Section: Markets
By: Priya Raghavan
Published: 2026-10-28T13:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-28T13:00:00Z

Jio Platforms opened 21% above its ₹1,119 IPO price on Wednesday and closed at ₹1,419 after India's largest offering, which sold about 3% of the company.

Jio Platforms, Reliance Industries' telecoms and digital arm, opened at ₹1,358 on its debut on Wednesday, 21.36 per cent above its ₹1,119 offer price, after raising ₹30,213 crore in India's largest initial public offering, according to Upstox's listing-day coverage.
The shares, which trade on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) under the symbol JPL and on BSE, moved between ₹1,357 and ₹1,374.50 in the morning before rising in the afternoon and settling at ₹1,419 on the NSE, up 4.49 per cent on the opening price and, by our arithmetic, 26.8 per cent above the offer price. Upstox put the closing market value at ₹13,05,380.12 crore, or about ₹13.05 lakh crore (₹13.05tn). TechCrunch reported that the opening price valued Jio at about $131.9bn, making it India's second-most valuable listed company after its parent.
The offering was entirely new shares, 27 crore of them, priced at the top of a ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 range, with no existing investor selling. It opened on Wednesday 21 October and closed on Friday 23 October, Upstox reported, and was subscribed 22.19 times. TechCrunch put investor bids at more than $77bn from more than 13.8 million applicants. The issue surpassed Hyundai Motor India's 2024 offering as the country's largest, according to Upstox and Business Today. Anchor investors, Upstox reported, included LIC, BlackRock, Fidelity, J.P. Morgan, Capital Group and the Government of Singapore.
Most of the money is earmarked for debt. Up to ₹275bn, about 91 per cent of the proceeds by our arithmetic, will repay borrowings at the subsidiary Reliance Jio Infocomm, TechCrunch reported, against total borrowings of ₹613.7bn at the end of June. If all of it is used that way, that would retire about 45 per cent of the borrowings, by our arithmetic.
Akash Ambani, Jio's managing director, told employees the listing "is not our destination" but "a new beginning", according to Upstox. TechCrunch quoted him saying: "My dream is that one day, when the world counts its great technology companies, one of them will be from India." He said the platforms serve more than 540 million customers.
The float is the detail the headline numbers leave out. Dividing the closing market value by the closing price gives about 920 crore shares in issue, by our arithmetic; the 27 crore new shares are about 2.9 per cent of that. An offering that drew more than $77bn of bids was, in other words, a sale of less than a thirtieth of the company, and the first-day price was set by trading in that sliver.

# Guidewire pays $1.7bn for an underwriting start-up

URL: https://kompositenews.com/fintech/guidewire-pays-1-7bn-for-an-underwriting-start-up/
Section: Fintech
By: Elena Vasquez
Published: 2026-10-28T12:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-10-28T12:40:00Z

Guidewire agreed to buy London underwriting-software firm hyperexponential for $1.7bn in cash plus up to $400m, funded partly by a $1bn loan.

Guidewire, a US maker of software for property and casualty insurers, agreed on Tuesday to buy hyperexponential, a London developer of AI underwriting software, for $1.7bn in cash plus up to $400m if revenue targets are met, the company said.
According to the announcement, made at Guidewire's Connections conference in Las Vegas, the base price is subject to adjustments, and the contingent payment of up to $400m depends on specified recurring revenue targets. Guidewire will fund the deal with $1.0bn of new term loan financing, committed by Bank of America and Citibank, and cash on hand. It expects the deal to close in the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year. Centerview Partners advised Guidewire and J.P. Morgan advised hyperexponential.
Hyperexponential, known as hx, sells software that commercial insurers use to build pricing models and make underwriting decisions. The company says its platform has supported underwriting across more than $75bn of annual commercial premium, and names Aviva, Allianz, Sompo, Beazley, Markel, HDI and Cincinnati Financial among its customers. It was already a Guidewire technology partner. TechCrunch reported that hx was founded in 2017, has raised nearly $90m, according to PitchBook, from investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Battery Ventures, and that nearly 600 insurers in 40 countries use its software.
Amrit Santhirasenan, hx's chief executive and co-founder, said in the release that the company was founded "on the conviction that underwriting judgment is the highest-leverage work insurers do". Mike Rosenbaum, Guidewire's chief executive, said: "We're delighted to welcome Amrit Santhirasenan and the team at hyperexponential to Guidewire." TechCrunch described the aim as putting AI agents to work alongside human underwriters on analysis and pricing decisions.
Guidewire did not disclose hx's revenue, but its guidance allows an estimate. It said the deal will add at least 650 basis points to its fiscal 2027 growth in annual recurring revenue (ARR), the yearly value of subscription contracts, on an inorganic basis, and at least 150 basis points a year to organic growth from fiscal 2028. Guidewire ended fiscal 2026 with ARR of $1,242m, or $1,237m at July 2026 exchange rates, its results release says. Applying 6.5 percentage points to that base implies about $80m of ARR from hx, by our arithmetic. On that estimate the base price is about 21 times hx's recurring revenue, and about 26 times if the full earnout is paid.

The implied ARR uses Guidewire's floor of 650 basis points and is an estimate, not a disclosed figure.The estimate has limits: 650 basis points is a floor, the ARR may be counted on Guidewire's definition rather than hx's, and the timing of the close will affect how much lands in fiscal 2027. The deal also changes Guidewire's balance sheet. By our subtraction, the cash portion of the base price is about $700m, more than half of the $1,215.3m in cash and investments Guidewire held at the end of July. The company said the deal will not affect its first-quarter guidance and that it will update its full-year forecast on its December earnings call.
Why it matters: underwriting and pricing are where insurers make or lose money, and the deal puts a specialist pricing tool inside software that many carriers already use to run policies and claims. For hx's investors, TechCrunch noted, it is a large return; by our arithmetic the base price is about 19 times the capital the company has raised.
Komposite has reported on how claims processing and other back-office work became a proving ground for agentic software, and on the spread of parametric insurance, where payouts follow measured events rather than adjusted claims. Guidewire's offer puts a price on the underwriting end of the same shift.
